title: Integrated Causal Reasoning Assessment: Two Foresters
description: Assesses student understanding of cooperation, social dilemmas, and sustainable resource use in a simple two-agent system.

vignette.title: The Two Neighbors
vignette.text:
Maya and Carlos are neighbors who each own a small forest. They can harvest trees from their own forest, or they can also harvest from their neighbor's forest if they choose.

Each tree harvested provides 10 units of wood (valuable for building and selling). However, when a tree is harvested, it takes time to regrow. If too many trees are harvested too quickly, the forest cannot recover and both neighbors suffer.

Maya and Carlos must decide how many trees to harvest each year. They can communicate and make agreements, but they cannot force each other to follow any rules.

items.question: If Maya and Carlos both harvest 5 trees per year from their own forests, and the forests can regrow 5 trees per year, what will happen over time?

options.text: Both forests will be depleted because harvesting any trees is unsustainable.
options.misconception: Assumes all harvesting is unsustainable, ignores balance between harvest and regrowth.

options.text: Both forests will remain stable because harvest equals regrowth.
options.explanation: Recognizes that sustainability depends on the balance between harvest rate and regrowth rate.

options.text: One forest will grow while the other shrinks, depending on who harvests more.
options.misconception: Assumes competition rather than independent dynamics when each harvests from their own forest.

options.text: The forests will eventually disappear because trees cannot regrow fast enough.
options.misconception: Ignores the specific balance between harvest and regrowth rates.

items.question: Maya suggests: 'Let's both agree to harvest only 3 trees per year so our forests grow healthier.' Carlos agrees but then secretly harvests 7 trees that year while Maya harvests only 3. What is the most likely outcome?

options.text: Carlos will have more wood this year, but both forests will be worse off in the long run.
options.explanation: Recognizes the short-term benefit of cheating but the long-term cost to both parties from resource depletion.

options.text: Carlos will be better off in both the short and long term because he got more resources.
options.misconception: Ignores long-term consequences of resource depletion.

options.text: Maya will be better off because she followed the agreement and was honest.
options.misconception: Moral reasoning rather than ecological outcome - ignores resource dynamics.

options.text: Both will be equally well off because the total harvest is the same (10 trees total).
options.misconception: Ignores that the distribution of harvest matters for forest health and future sustainability.

items.competencyTarget: Understanding social dilemmas and temptation to defect

items.question: After Carlos breaks their agreement, Maya discovers what happened. She has three options: (1) Continue harvesting only 3 trees, (2) Start harvesting 7 trees too, or (3) Harvest 10 trees to 'get back' at Carlos. Which option is most likely to lead to the best long-term outcome for both?

options.text: Option 1 - Continue harvesting only 3 trees to show she is trustworthy.
options.misconception: Moral reasoning that ignores the reality that unilateral cooperation leads to exploitation.

options.text: Option 2 - Start harvesting 7 trees to match Carlos's behavior.
options.explanation: Recognizes that matching the other's behavior can create a new equilibrium, though it may not be optimal.

options.text: Option 3 - Harvest 10 trees to punish Carlos for breaking the agreement.
options.misconception: Punishment logic that accelerates resource depletion and harms both parties.

options.text: None of these options will work - once trust is broken, cooperation is impossible.
options.misconception: Deterministic view of human relationships that ignores possibility of rebuilding trust through communication and new agreements.

items.competencyTarget: Understanding responses to defection and equilibrium dynamics

items.question: A student says: 'The problem is that Carlos is selfish. If everyone were just honest, there would be no problem.' What is the most accurate response from an evolutionary and systems thinking perspective?

options.text: The student is right - the problem is individual selfishness, not the structure of the situation.
options.misconception: Individual-blame framing that ignores systemic structure and incentives.

options.text: The problem is that forests regrow too slowly - we need faster-growing trees.
options.misconception: Technological fix that ignores the fundamental social dilemma structure.

options.text: The situation creates a dilemma where individual rational choices can lead to collectively poor outcomes, regardless of personal character.
options.explanation: Recognizes that social dilemmas emerge from the structure of incentives and payoffs, not from individual moral character.

options.text: The problem is that Maya and Carlos don't have a government to force them to cooperate.
options.misconception: External authority framing that ignores the possibility of self-organized cooperation.

items.competencyTarget: Understanding systemic structure vs. individual blame

items.question: How does changing the regrowth rate of the trees affect the cooperation dilemma?

options.text: It doesn't affect the dilemma - cooperation is always about trust and honesty.
options.misconception: Ignores how ecological parameters change the payoff structure of the social dilemma.

options.text: Faster regrowth makes cooperation less necessary because there are more resources to go around.
options.explanation: Recognizes that ecological parameters (regrowth rate) change the payoff structure, affecting how severe the dilemma is.

options.text: Slower regrowth makes cooperation easier because people are more careful with scarce resources.
options.misconception: Assumes scarcity automatically leads to cooperation, ignoring that scarcity can also increase competition.

options.text: Regrowth rate only affects individual forests, not the cooperation between Maya and Carlos.
options.misconception: False separation between ecological and social systems.

items.competencyTarget: Understanding how ecological parameters affect social dilemmas

integratedReasoning.description: Student recognizes systemic structure, payoff dynamics, and the interaction between ecological and social factors.
indicators: Understands balance between harvest and regrowth
Understands how parameters affect dilemma structure

dichotomizedReasoning.description: Student relies on moral reasoning, individual blame, or ignores systemic structure and dynamics.
indicators: Frames problems in terms of individual character

commonMisconceptions: Individual blame: Attributing problems to selfishness rather than systemic structure
Moral reasoning: Using moral categories instead of analyzing payoffs and outcomes
Technological optimism: Assuming technical fixes can solve social dilemmas
Determinism: Assuming relationships cannot change after trust is broken
suggestedActivities: Run the model with different regrowth rates and observe outcomes
Compare private vs. shared resource scenarios
Discuss real-world examples of cooperation dilemmas (climate change, fisheries, etc.)
Use payoff matrices to analyze different scenarios
connectionsToOtherModels: population-size-living-costs: Explore effects of more agents
